source.title: Feature Drift: How Fine-Tuning Repurposes Representations in LLMs
source.authors: Andrey V. Galichin; Anton Korznikov; Alexey Dontsov; Oleg Y. Rogov; Elena Tutubalina; I. Oseledets

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies drift in sparse-autoencoder features during fine-tuning, not neuron poles, neuron explanation accuracy, or attribution graphs built from a model’s own neurons. Its results do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: No results test the listed neuron-pole or neuron-explanation claims. The paper reports its own results about SAE-feature transfer, feature drift, and refusal interventions; these are recorded as related but distinct findings under versions ["none"]. Results from cited prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies SAE feature transfer and drift between base and chat models, plus refusal interventions with SAE features. It audits no neuron poles, scores no neuron explanations, builds no neuron attribution graphs and studies no vision neurons. None of its results bear on V1–V7. Relation is closer to cites_only than discusses: the paper never addresses neuron monosemanticity or the essay's claims. It only cites SAE interpretability work in passing.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that instruction tuning shifts when existing SAE features activate rather than creating new ones: base SAEs transfer with 7–9% FVU degradation, and similarity of activations does not explain this alone. Drifted features causally mediate refusal in Gemma-2-2B-IT. They call the account more complete but not exhaustive.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares sparse-autoencoder features across base and chat models and intervenes on reconstructed refusal directions. It does not audit neuron poles or test explanations of individual neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports results across model families and early, middle, and late layers; the Qwen2.5 models show minimal transfer degradation. Refusal intervention outcomes vary with feature source and k.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-model SAEs reconstruct chat-model activations with about 7–9% FVU degradation. The sets of active features differ across paired tokens (IR 0.1–0.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning repurposes existing SAE features (feature drift) rather than creating new ones. This concerns SAE dictionary features, not neuron poles.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-2B-IT, refusal directions rebuilt from chat-selected SAE features control refusal far more than base-selected ones (safety about 0.1 vs 0.7; induced refusal about 50% vs below 5%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features that drift to fire on harmful prompts causally mediate refusal in chat models.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of EACL 2026)
record.problems: For the neuron-pole claims, the study tests no neuron-level job audit or explanation-prediction metric. Its refusal causal validation is limited to one model family and one behavior; the authors note its feature-selection method has limited fidelity (Cos = 0.51 at k = 64) and that chat SAEs were trained on fewer tokens than base SAEs (0.5B versus 2B). Several cross-model metrics are reported only as ranges or aggregate descriptions.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual model-layer points in Figures 1 and 3 because the text gives aggregate descriptions and ranges rather than extractable values for each point. Table 1's direction reconstruction metrics are not included because they do not measure a listed claim version or add a distinct finding about neuron job interpretability.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (about 90% one job, 7% two, 2–4% unknown).
Neuron job shares across other models, dense and MoE, and scale.
InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons and the recursive generalization versus superposition question.
How architecture, regularization and tools affect the interpretable-neuron share.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are fine as non-claim rows, and all versions are correctly set to ['none']. The relation should be cites_only rather than discusses, since the paper never engages neuron-level interpretability claims.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and the proportions of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Neuron-pole job shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Neuron interpretability rates across architectures, regularization choices, tools, and vision models.
Whether attribution graphs made from a large model’s own neurons explain behavior without replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples fail to predict neuron activation on new examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

conditions.value: six listed model pairs; aggregate result
B-LLM + B-Data; B-LLM + C-Data; C-LLM + C-Data

rows.measure: Fraction of variance unexplained (FVU) degradation for transferred base SAEs.
rows.baseline: B-LLM + B-Data; the text reports approximately 5% increase in FVU on changing to chat data, then a further 2–3% on changing to chat-model activations.
rows.value: 7–8% performance degradation for base SAEs applied to chat models with chat data; approximately 9% degradation relative to chat SAEs.
rows.note: The paper reports these aggregate comparisons across the tested model families and layer depths. This concerns SAE reconstruction, not the listed neuron-pole claims.
rows.check: SAE reconstruction (FVU) transfer, not neuron interpretability. The baseline field mixes a step value (5%) with the comparison. Qwen2.5 shows minimal degradation, which the aggregate range hides.

source_check.problem: Baseline field mixes the ~5% base-to-chat-data step with the comparison; text also gives ~9% vs chat SAEs and minimal degradation for Qwen2.5.

relation.reason: The paper doesn't engage the neuron claim and doesn't cite its original. cites_only is the weakest available category and fits; the reader's 'discusses' would overstate the link.

tranche.reason: SAE feature transfer/drift and refusal interventions with SAE features; no neuron poles audited, no neuron explanations scored, no neuron attribution graphs, no vision neurons. It neither tests nor uses V1-V7.

source_check.notes: All 7 rows match the text. This is an off-topic SAE-feature study (base-to-chat SAE transfer and refusal), with no neuron-level results. R1's aggregate 7-8% (about 9% vs chat SAEs) hides the minimal degradation for Qwen2.5. The pre-ablation safety score of 1.0 in R4/R5 is implied by the conclusion, not shown as a separate control.
